title: Citadel: Rethinking Memory Allocation to Safeguard Against Inter-Domain Rowhammer Exploits
problem: Rowhammer attacks exploit DRAM's physical row-adjacency to corrupt memory rows belonging to different security domains; hardware mitigations are costly, slow to adopt, and repeatedly circumvented, while software mitigations incur large performance and memory capacity overheads or provide only partial protection.
motivation: DRAM density continues to increase, raising Rowhammer attack probability; cloud and server systems host thousands of isolated tenants sharing physical memory, and no existing approach simultaneously provides comprehensive cross-domain isolation, low overhead, and broad platform compatibility.
method: Citadel is a software memory allocator that prevents Rowhammer attacks (exploits where repeated memory access corrupts nearby DRAM rows) by physically isolating different security domains—separate applications or users—in distant memory regions so they never occupy adjacent rows. It works by tracking the physical layout of rows in DRAM and partitioning the address space (the mapping of memory addresses to physical locations) so domain boundaries are always separated by guard rows or page-aligned gaps. The system supports thousands of simultaneous security domains with only 7.2% additional memory overhead and no measurable performance loss, while working on any DRAM platform without requiring hardware modifications.
key_novelty: Citadel prevents cross-domain Rowhammer attacks using a software memory allocator that physically isolates security domains in separate DRAM regions, providing protection without hardware modifications, performance loss, or the excessive overhead of earlier approaches.
contributions: Citadel memory allocator: security-by-design through physical domain isolation in disjoint DRAM regions
Support for thousands of security domains at only 7.2% average memory overhead with no performance loss
Flexible security domain abstraction compatible with legacy, contemporary, and future platforms without hardware changes
4-6x lower overhead than recent domain isolation schemes for supported workload scenarios
